chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Mahfuz al-Iskaaf, who said:

I saw Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) throw pebbles at the Jamarat al-Aqaba and then depart. So I walked in front of him like a path-clearer for him. And behold, a pale man, an Amraki, had inserted a peg into the ground, resembling a settler, and tied it to his tent. The people were standing, unable to pass. So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'O this man, fear Allah, for that which you are doing is not for you.'

He (the narrator) said, So the Amraki said to him: 'Can't you just go about your work? The one who is burdened (with the duty of forbidding evil), whose identity is unknown, keeps coming to me saying: O this man, fear Allah.'
He (the narrator) said, So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) raised the halter of a camel of his that was tied, lowered his head, and passed by. And the Amraki, the slave, left him.

key_terms.الْعَمْرَكِيُّ: Amraki (a type of slave or servant, often used to denote a specific status)
key_terms.الْمُكَلَّفُ: The one burdened (with the duty of commanding good and forbidding evil)
key_terms.جَمْرَةَ الْعَقَبَةِ: Jamarat al-Aqaba (the large stone pillar at Mina where pilgrims throw pebbles)
key_terms.عُودَةً: A peg or stake used to secure a tent

ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) demonstrate the concept of denying evil by the heart in this incident?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the nuanced application of *Amr bil Ma'ruf* (commanding good) by Imam al-Sadiq (AS) during Hajj, specifically addressing the condition of *Ghaybah* (occultation) or lack of public recognition. The 'yellow-skinned Amri' man’s retort highlights a common objection: that without a clearly identifiable authority, the duty of forbidding evil becomes a source of harassment rather than guidance. The Imam’s silent departure demonstrates the principle of *Denying Evil by the Heart* (when action is not feasible or appropriate), showing that patience and non-engagement with the obstinate are valid forms of spiritual resistance in Shia jurisprudence.
